title: 49  Biopython
text:
Sequence records
A SeqRecord is Biopython’s grown-up version of the simple Gene class you wrote in Chapter 38.

from Bio.SeqRecord import SeqRecord

record = SeqRecord(dna, id="N42", name="orf1", description="A made-up ORF")
print(record)

It has an id, a name and a description attribute. And it keeps a Seq object as its seq attribute. You access the attributes with the . operator (like p.x for the x-value for a point):

print(record.id)
print(record.description)
print(record.seq)

title: 49  Biopython
text:
Reading and writing sequence files
In the projects you read sequences from files by opening the files and reading one line at a time in a for loop. That works if each line contains one sequence. However, the most common sequence formats split each sequence record over multiple lines. The Fasta format is the simples one. Have a look at this Fasta record for the human FOXP2 gene. The first line begins with a “>” character and contains only a sequence id and an optional description. The sequence itself is split across lines below it. If you had to, I am sure you could produce code that would read and write Fasta records, but Biopython’s SeqIO module will do that for you and it reads and writes many other file formats too. Import it like this:

from Bio import SeqIO

You will rarely make a SeqRecord object yourself unless you produce some sequence data you want to use with Biopython. Lets pretend you have found three small ORFs in your project on finding open reading frames and want to write them to a file. You make a SeqRecord object for each one and put them in a list like this:

my_records = [
    SeqRecord(Seq("ATGGCCATTGTAATGGGCCGCTGA"), id="orf1", description="first"),
    SeqRecord(Seq("ATGAAACCCGGGTTTTAA"), id="orf2", description="second"),
    SeqRecord(Seq("ATGTGATAA"), id="orf3", description="third"),
]

Now you can pass the list to the write function defined in the SeqIO module along with the name of the file to write to and the name of the format you want, in this case “fasta”:

SeqIO.write(my_records, "my_orfs.fasta", "fasta")

SeqIO.write returned 3, the number of records it wrote to the file. You can see in the sidebar of VS Code that my_orfs.fasta was created. Open it in VS Code and have a look.
Now lets pretend you come back later and want to read it back into Python. You do that using SeqIOs parse function, which returns an object you can iterate over in a for loop.

for rec in SeqIO.parse("my_orfs.fasta", "fasta"):
    print(rec.id, len(rec), rec.seq.translate(to_stop=True))

SeqIO.parse reads one record at a time as the for-loop asks for it, just like a file object serves one line at a time (Section 30.0.0.5). If it read in all the records before handing each one to the for loop, a file with millions of records could fill up you computer’s memory. This way, you only keep one record in memory at a time. If you do want all the records at once, just then the value returned by SeqIO.parse into a list:

list(SeqIO.parse("my_orfs.fasta", "fasta"))


Exercise 49-7
SOLO
SeqIO has a sibling of parse called read, which you use when the file holds exactly one record. It then returns that record directly, so you do not need a loop. What do you think happens if you use read on a file with three records? Decide before you run it.

%%sandbox
from Bio import SeqIO

rec = SeqIO.read("my_orfs.fasta", "fasta")
print(rec.id)

title: 49  Biopython
text:
GenBank files
A FASTA file holds little more than names and sequences. A GenBank record holds a sequence together with all the associated information from the database. In the data folder of your instructing-machines folder, the NM_148900.4.gb file contains a GenBank record for the same FOXP2 sequence you looked at as a Fasta record above. Before you go on , have a look at it here or open it from the data folder in VS code. I am sure would would rather not have to parse that file yourself. To read a file with GenBank records, you just give SeqIO.parse "genbank" instead of "fasta" as its last argument:

for rec in SeqIO.parse("data/NM_148900.4.gb", "genbank"):
    print(rec.id)

For files like this one with only a single record in it, there is not point to the for loop. In that case, use the read function instead, which reads in that single record:

record = SeqIO.read("data/NM_148900.4.gb", "genbank")

To write the GenBank record to a file in Fasta format, you just use "fasta" as the third argument to SeqIO.write():

SeqIO.write(record, "NM_148900.4.fasta", "fasta")


Exercise 49-8
SOLO
The GenBank record has the same id, name, and description attributes as the Fasta records. The rest of the header of the file ends up in the annotations attribute, which is an ordinary dictionary. I am sure you remember the dictionary methods from Chapter 21, so you can easily list the keys this dictionary. What are they? Inspect the value associated with each one. Are they all strings, and if not, what types are they, and how do you dig into what is in them?


Sequence features
In the FOXP2 GenBank file, scroll down to the FEATURES section. It lists the exon, intron, CDS, and other regions of the sequence. Each one is read into a SeqFeature object and put in a list you can access as the features of the resulting sequence record.
Let us extract the coding sequence. Each SeqFeature object has the the following attributes: extract, id, location, qualifiers, translate, type. The type attribute says if the feature is a CDS, exon, intron, or something else. The code below loops over the features to extract a list of only the CDS features (in this case a single one):

cds_features = []
for feature in record.features:
    if feature.type == "CDS":
        cds_features.append(feature)

cds = cds_features[0] # extract the single CDS feature

Knowing the start and end indices, we could slice out the CDS, but you would need to check if it is on the negative strand in which case you would also need to reverse-complement the resulting sequence:

cds_seq = record.seq[cds.location.start:cds.location.end]
if cds.location.strand == '-':
    cds_seq = cds_seq.reverse_complement()
cds_seq

To make this common task easy, the sequence features have an extract method that extracts the feature’s sequence:

cds_seq = cds.extract(record.seq)
cds_seq


Exercise 49-9
SOLO
Each SeqFeature has a qualifiers attribute that holds a dictionary with additional information about the feature. For the CDS, one is the official translation. See if you can fish it out and then compare to it to what cds_seq.translate(to_stop=True) returns.


Exercise 49-10
SOLO
See if you can splice out the introns. It basically amounts to extracting and concatenating all features except the introns. Hint: Seq objects has a join method like strings so you can do: Seq('').join([Seq('ATG'), Seq('TAG')]) to produce Seq('ATGTAG').


Exercise 49-11
SOLO
Run the cell below:

record = SeqIO.read("data/NM_148900.4.gb", "genbank")
for feature in record.features:
    print(feature.type, feature.location)

The code print says the CDS is at [556:2755](+) (the (+) just says the feature is on the forward strand). Now open the GenBank file and find the line where the CDS starts. As you can see, the file says the CDS is at 557..2755, Is one of them wrong or are there more than one approach to enumerating positions?

title: 49  Biopython
text:
Fetching records from NCBI
If you wonder where that GenBank file came from, it was downloaded from NCBI’s nucleotide database, which you can search in the browser at ncbi.nlm.nih.gov along with many other databases.
Sometimes you want to automate that kind of data retrieval using Python code in a python script or notebook. The module Bio.Entrez lets your program do the same searches and downloads as you can do using a browser.
NCBI asks that you send at most three requests per second (Biopython makes sure of that for you), and if you need to send more than a hundred requests in a row, you should do it on a weekend or outside US office hours. You should provide your email address, so they can contact you if your program misbehaves, rather than just blocking requests from your computer.
The cell below downloads the record we have been using. Put your own email address in it before you run it.

from Bio import Entrez

Entrez.email = "your@post.au.dk"   # use your own address

handle = Entrez.efetch(db="nucleotide",  # database to search
                       id="NM_148900.4", # id of sequence to download
                       rettype="gb",     # format of downloaded record
                       retmode="text") 

# read from the handle as you would from a file
seq_record = SeqIO.read(handle, "genbank")

# write the record to a file on your harddisk
SeqIO.write(seq_record, "NM_148900.4.gb", "genbank")

If you do not know the accession number (here NM_148900.4), you can search database enntries with Entrez.esearch. The search term uses the same syntax as the search box on the NCBI website, and Entrez.read turns NCBI’s answer into a dictionary:

handle = Entrez.esearch(
    db="nucleotide", 
    term="FOXP2[Gene] AND Homo sapiens[Organism] AND srcdb_refseq[prop]", 
    retmax=10)

result = Entrez.read(handle)

Then you use the get the records found to see what they are:

for seq_id in result["IdList"]:
    handle = Entrez.efetch(db="nucleotide", id=seq_id, rettype="gb", retmode="text") 
    record = SeqIO.read(handle, "genbank")
    print(record.id, record.description)


Exercise 49-12
SOLO
Change the search so it finds the FOXP2 sequences of the chimpanzee (Pan troglodytes) instead. Then fetch one of them with Entrez.efetch, read it with SeqIO.read, and print its description and length.


Exercise 49-13
AI: Explainer
The search term above contains srcdb_refseq[prop]. Ask the assistant what that part of the term means and what would change if you left it out. Then settle it by running the search with and without it and comparing the two values of result["Count"].

title: 49  Biopython
text:
Pairwise alignment
We will revisit the top of alignment later in the course, but we include a bit on alignment here because it is also part of Biopython. You make a PairwiseAligner object and then use its align method to align two sequences:

from Bio import Align

aligner = Align.PairwiseAligner()
alignments = aligner.align("GAACT", "GAT")

print(alignments.score)
print(len(alignments))
for alignment in alignments:
    print(alignment)

There are two different alignments with the same, best score, and the aligner gives you both. The numbers in the margins are positions in each sequence, counted Python’s way from 0.
The score comes from the aligner’s scoring settings, which are attributes on the aligner object. By default a match scores 1, a mismatch scores 0, and every gap position scores -1:

print(aligner.match_score)
print(aligner.mismatch_score)
print(aligner.open_gap_score)
print(aligner.extend_gap_score)


Exercise 49-14
SOLO
Use the four scores above to compute the score of each of the two alignments by hand, position by position, the way you would do substitution and reduction steps: replace each column by its score, then add them up. Do you get the score the aligner printed?
Change the attributes and you change the alignment. Setting mode to "local" asks for the best-scoring part of the two sequences rather than the whole of both. For proteins, you usually score with a substitution matrix like BLOSUM62, which gives similar amino acids a positive score even if they are not identical:

from Bio.Align import substitution_matrices

protein_aligner = Align.PairwiseAligner()
protein_aligner.mode = "local"
protein_aligner.substitution_matrix = substitution_matrices.load("BLOSUM62")
protein_aligner.open_gap_score = -10
protein_aligner.extend_gap_score = -0.5

best = protein_aligner.align("HEAGAWGHEE", "PAWHEAE")[0]
print(best.score)
print(best)



Exercise 49-15
AI: Explainer
Look at the line in the middle of a printed alignment, the one made of |, . and -. Ask the assistant what each of the three symbols means. Then check its answer against one of the alignments you printed yourself, column by column. In the protein alignment, is every . really a mismatch between two different amino acids?

title: 50  Project: Genome assembly
text:
Read and analyze the sequencing reads
This chapter is a programming project where you will assemble a small genomic sequence from a set of short sequencing reads.
In genome assembly, many short sequences (reads) from a sequencing machine are assembled into long sequences – ultimately chromosomes. This is done by ordering overlapping reads so that they together represent genomic sequences. For example, given these three reads: AGGTCGTAG, CGTAGAGCTGGGAG, GGGAGGTTGAAA, ordering them based on their overlap like this
produces the following genomic sequence:
Real genome assembly is, of course, more sophisticated than what we do here, but the idea is the same. To limit the complexity of the problem, we make two simplifying assumptions:
The second assumption implies that overlaps are always of this type:
and never of this type:
In this project, you will be asked to write functions that solve the problem of assembling a genomic sequence. Each function solves a small problem, and you may need to call these functions inside other functions to put together solutions to larger subproblems.
Begin by downloading the project. Open your instructing machines folder in VS Code. Then open a terminal (Terminal > New Terminal from the top menu) and run this command:
That puts the assemblyproject project folder straight into the projects folder inside your course folder, beside your notebooks.
If that fails, you can always click “Download project” in the top right corner of the page. This downloads a zip file to your Downloads folder that you need to then unpack and move into the projects folder of your student folder yourself.
You write your code in the file called assemblyproject.py. In the terminal, navigate to the project folder and run your code in the usual way:
To test the functions as you complete each one, you use pytest to run the project test suite in test_assemblyproject.py using this command:
Now open each file in your editor and look at what is in sequencing_reads.txt. (Do not change it in any way, and do not save it after viewing. If your editor asks you if you want to save it before closing, say no.) How many sequences are there in each file?
The project is split into four parts:
Here is an overview of the functions you will write in each part of the project and of which functions are used by other functions.
Make sure to read the entire exercise and understand what you are supposed to do before you begin!
The first task is to read and parse the input data. The sequence reads for the mini-assembly are in the file sequencing_reads.txt. The first two lines of the file look like this:
Each line represents a read. The first field on each line is the name of the read, and the second field is the read sequence itself. So for the first line, Read1 is the name, and ATGCG... is the sequence.

title: 50  Project: Genome assembly
text:
Read1 GGCTCCCCACGGGGTACCCATAACTTGACAGTAGATCTCGTCCAGACCCCTAGC
Read2 CTTTACCCGGAAGAGCGGGACGCTGCCCTGCGCGATTCCAGGCTCCCCACGGG


Read the sequencing reads into your program
Write a function, read_data, that takes one argument:

A string, which is the name of the data file.

The function must return

A dictionary, where the keys are the names of reads and the values are the associated read sequences. Both keys and values must be strings.

Example usage:
read_data('sequencing_reads.txt')
should return a dictionary with the following content (maybe not with key-value pairs in that order)
{'Read1': 'GGCTCCCCACGGGGTACCCATAACTTGACAGTAGATCTCGTCCAGACCCCTAGC',
 'Read3': 'GTCTTCAGTAGAAAATTGTTTTTTTCTTCCAAGAGGTCGGAGTCGTGAACACATCAGT',
 'Read2': 'CTTTACCCGGAAGAGCGGGACGCTGCCCTGCGCGATTCCAGGCTCCCCACGGG',
 'Read5': 'CGATTCCAGGCTCCCCACGGGGTACCCATAACTTGACAGTAGATCTC',
 'Read4': 'TGCGAGGGAAGTGAAGTATTTGACCCTTTACCCGGAAGAGCG',
 'Read6': 'TGACAGTAGATCTCGTCCAGACCCCTAGCTGGTACGTCTTCAGTAGAAAATTGTTTTTTTCTTCCAAGAGGTCGGAGT'}
Here is some scaffolding code to get you started:
def read_data(file_name):
    input_file = open(file_name)
    # ...
    for line in input_file:
         # ...    
    # ...
    
    input_file.close() 
    
The line variable in the for loop holds each line in the file, including the \n newline character at the end. You can use the’ split’ method of strings to split each line into the name of the read and the read sequence. You can see the documentation for that method by typing pydoc str.split in your terminal.


Compute the mean length of reads
After writing that function, we would like to get an idea about the length of the reads. There are often too many reads to look at manually, so we need to make a function that computes the mean length of the reads.
Write a function, mean_length, that takes one argument:

A dictionary, in which keys are read names and values are read sequences (this is a dictionary like that returned by read_data).

The function must return

A float, which is the average length of the sequence reads.

One way to do this is to loop over the keys in the dictionary like this:
def mean_length(reads):
    count = 0
    total = 0
    for name in reads:
        seq = reads[name]
        # ...
        # ...
    # ...
    return total / count
Remember that you can use the len function to find the length of a read.

title: 50  Project: Genome assembly
text:
Compute overlaps between reads
The next step is to determine which reads overlap each other. We need a function that takes two read sequences and computes their overlap to do that. Remember that in the input data, none of the reads are completely nested in another read.

Compute the overlap between two reads
We know there are no sequencing errors so that the sequence match will be perfect in the overlap. To compute the overlap between the 3’ (right) end of the left read with the 5’ (left) end of the righthand read, you need to loop over all possible overlaps, honoring that one sequence is the left one and the other is the right one. In the for loop, start with the largest possible overlap ( min(len(left), len(right))) and evaluate smaller and smaller overlaps until you find an exact match.
Write a function, get_overlap, that takes two arguments

A string, which is the lefthand read sequence.
A string, which is the righthand read sequence.

The function must return

A string, which is the overlapping sequence. If there is no overlap, it should return an empty string.

Example usage:
s1 = "CGATTCCAGGCTCCCCACGGGGTACCCATAACTTGACAGTAGATCTC"
s2 = "GGCTCCCCACGGGGTACCCATAACTTGACAGTAGATCTCGTCCAGACCCCTAGC"
get_overlap(s1, s2)
should return the string
'GGCTCCCCACGGGGTACCCATAACTTGACAGTAGATCTC'
and get_overlap(s2, s1)
should return the string
'C'
From these two examples, it seems that s1 and s2 overlap and that s1 is the left and s2 is the right. Treating s2 as the left one and s1 as the right one only gives an overlap of one base (we expect a few bases of overlap even for unrelated sequences).




Compute all read overlaps
When you have written get_overlap, you can use it to evaluate the overlap between all pairs of reads in both left-right and right-left orientations.
Write a function, get_all_overlaps, that takes one argument:

A dictionary with read data as returned by read_data.

The function must return

A dictionary of dictionaries specifying the number of overlapping bases for a pair of reads in a specific left-right orientation. Computing the overlap of a read to itself is meaningless and must not be included. Assuming the resulting dictionary of dictionaries is called d, then d['Read2'] will be a dictionary where keys are the names of reads that have an overlap with read 'Read2' when 'Read2' is put in the left position, and the values for these keys are the number of overlapping bases for those reads.

Example usage: assuming that reads is a dictionary returned by read_data then:
get_all_overlaps(reads)
should return the following dictionary of dictionaries (but not necessarily with the same ordering of the key-value pairs):
{'Read1': {'Read3': 0, 'Read2': 1, 'Read5': 1, 'Read4': 0, 'Read6': 29},
 'Read3': {'Read1': 0, 'Read2': 0, 'Read5': 0, 'Read4': 1, 'Read6': 1},
 'Read2': {'Read1': 13, 'Read3': 1, 'Read5': 21, 'Read4': 0, 'Read6': 0},
 'Read5': {'Read1': 39, 'Read3': 0, 'Read2': 1, 'Read4': 0, 'Read6': 14},
 'Read4': {'Read1': 1, 'Read3': 1, 'Read2': 17, 'Read5': 2, 'Read6': 0},
 'Read6': {'Read1': 0, 'Read3': 43, 'Read2': 0, 'Read5': 0, 'Read4': 1}}






NoteHint





You can use the get_overlap function you just made to find the overlap between a pair of reads. To generate all combinations of reads, you need two for-loops. One looping over reads in the left position, and another (inside the first one) looping over reads in the right position. Remember that we do not want the overlap of a read to itself, so there should be an if-statement checking that the left and right reads are not the same.





Print overlaps as a nice table
The dictionary returned by get_all_overlaps is a bit messy. We want to print it in a nice matrix-like format so we can better see which pairs overlap in which orientations.
This pretty_print function should take one argument:

A dictionary of dictionaries as returned by get_all_overlaps.

The function should not return anything but must print a matrix exactly as shown in the example below with nicely aligned and right-justified columns. The first column must hold names of reads in left orientation. The top row holds names of reads in right orientation. The remaining cells must each have the number of overlapping bases for a left-right read pair. The diagonal corresponds to overlaps with the read itself. You must put dashes in these cells.
Example usage: assuming that overlaps is a dictionary of dictionaries returned by get_all_overlaps then:
pretty_print(overlaps)
should print exactly
       Read1  Read2  Read3  Read4  Read5  Read6 
Read1      -      1      0      0      1     29 
Read2     13      -      1      0     21      0
Read3      0      0      -      1      0      1
Read4      1     17      1      -      2      0 
Read5     39      1      0      0      -     14 
Read6      0      0     43      1      0      -
This function is hard to get completely right. So, to spare you the frustration, this one is on me:
def pretty_print(d):
    print('      ', end='')
    for j in sorted(d):
        print("{: >6}".format(j), end='')
    print()
    for i in sorted(d):
        print("{: >6}".format(i), end='')
        for j in sorted(d):
            if i == j:
                s = '     -'
            else:
                s = "{: >6}".format(d[str(i)][str(j)])
            print(s, end='')
        print()
Make sure you understand how it works. You can look up in the documentation what "{: >6}".format(i) does.

title: 50  Project: Genome assembly
section: Find the correct order of reads
text:
Find the correct order of reads
Now that we know how the reads overlap, we can chain them pair by pair from left to right to get the order in which they represent the genomic sequence. To do this, we take the first (left-most) read and identify which read has the largest overlap at its right end. Then we take that read and find the read with the largest overlap to the right end of that - until we reach the rightmost (last) read.

Find the first read
The first thing you need to do is to identify the first (leftmost) read so we know where to start. This read is identified as the one that has no significant (>2) overlaps to its left end (it only has a good overlap when positioned to the left of other reads). In the example output from pretty_print above, the first read would be read 'Read4' because the 'Read4' column has no significant overlaps (no one larger than two).
We break the problem in two and first write a function that gets all the overlaps to the left end of a read (i.e., when it is in the right position):
Write a function, get_left_overlaps, that takes two arguments:

A dictionary of dictionaries as returned from get_all_overlaps.
A string, which represents the name of a read.

The function must return

A sorted list of integers, which represent the overlaps of other reads to its left end.

Example usage: assuming that overlaps is a dictionary of dictionaries returned by get_all_overlaps then.
get_left_overlaps(overlaps, 'Read1')
should return
[0, 0, 1, 13, 39]






NoteHint





Once you have made a list of left overlaps, you can use the built-in function sorted to make a sorted version of the list that you can return from the function.



OK, now that we have a function that can find all the overlaps to the left end of a given read, all we need to do is find the particular read with no significant (>2) overlaps to its left end.
Write a function, find_first_read, that takes one argument:

A dictionary of dictionaries as returned from get_all_overlaps.

The function must return

A string containing the name of the first read.

Example usage: assuming that overlaps is a dictionary of dictionaries returned by get_all_overlaps then.
find_first_read(overlaps)
should return
'Read4'


Find the order of reads
Now that we have the first read, we can find the correct order of the reads. We want a list of the read names in the right order.
Given the first (left) read, the next read is the one that has the largest overlap to the right end of that read. We use our dictionary of overlaps to figure out which read that is. If the first read is 'Read4', then overlaps['Read4'] is a dictionary of reads with overlap to the right end of read 'Read4'. So, to find the name of the read with the largest overlap, you must write a function that finds the key associated with the largest value in a dictionary. We do that first:
Write a function, find_key_for_largest_value, that takes one argument:

A dictionary.

The function must return the key associated with the largest value in the dictionary argument.
Having written find_key_for_largest_value, you can use it as a tool in the function that finds the order of reads:
Write a function, find_order_of_reads, that takes two arguments:

A string, which is the name of the first (left-most) read (that is returned by find_first_read).
A dictionary of dictionaries of all overlaps (that returned by get_all_overlaps).

The function must return

A list of strings, which are read names in the order in which they represent the genomic sequence.







NoteHint





You know the first read is given by the first argument to the function. You also know that you can find the next read in the chain of overlapping reads by using the find_key_for_largest_value function. You should keep adding reads to the chain as long as the overlap is larger than two (you can use a for loop with an if statement inside to check that the overlap is larger than 2).



Example usage: assuming that overlaps is a dictionary of dictionaries returned by get_all_overlaps then:
find_order_of_reads('Read4', overlaps)
should return:
['Read4', 'Read2', 'Read5', 'Read1', 'Read6', 'Read3']
Before you implement the function, make sure you understand why this is the right list of read names.

title: 50  Project: Genome assembly
text:
Reconstruct the genomic sequence
Now that you have the number of overlapping bases between reads and the correct order of the reads, you can reconstruct the genomic sequence.

Reconstruct the genomic sequence from the reads
Write a function, reconstruct_sequence, that takes three arguments:

A list of strings, which are the names of reads in the order identified by find_order_of_reads.
A dictionary, with read data as returned from read_data.
A dictionary of dictionaries with overlaps as returned from get_all_overlaps.

The function must return

A string, which is the genomic sequence.

Example usage: assuming that order is the list of strings returned by find_order_of_reads, that reads is the dictionary returned by read_data and that overlaps is a dictionary of dictionaries returned by get_all_overlaps then:
reconstruct_sequence(order, reads, overlaps)    
should return one long DNA string (I had to break it in three to make it fit on the page):
TGCGAGGGAAGTGAAGTATTTGACCCTTTACCCGGAAGAGCGGGACGCTGCCCTGCGCGATT
CCAGGCTCCCCACGGGGTACCCATAACTTGACAGTAGATCTCGTCCAGACCCCTAGCTGGTA
CGTCTTCAGTAGAAAATTGTTTTTTTCTTCCAAGAGGTCGGAGTCGTGAACACATCAGT






NoteHint





Iterate over the reads in order and use the overlap information to extract and join the appropriate parts of the reads.





Putting the whole thing together
Now that you have written functions to handle each step, you can write one last function that uses them to complete the entire assembly.
Write a function, assemble_genome, that takes one argument:

A string, which is the name of a file with sequencing reads in the format described at the beginning of this project description.

The function must return

A string, which is the genome assembled from the sequencing reads

Example usage:
assemble_genome('sequencing_reads.txt')
should return the assembled genome:
TGCGAGGGAAGTGAAGTATTTGACCCTTTACCCGGAAGAGCGGGACGCTGCCCTGCGCGATT
CCAGGCTCCCCACGGGGTACCCATAACTTGACAGTAGATCTCGTCCAGACCCCTAGCTGGTA
CGTCTTCAGTAGAAAATTGTTTTTTTCTTCCAAGAGGTCGGAGTCGTGAACACATCAGT

title: 51  AI: Plan before you prompt
text:
By now you can specify a single function by writing its contract as tests, and you can read a single function the assistant produced and judge whether it keeps that contract. Both of those skills are about one function at a time. Real problems are not one function. The tasks you will tackle for the rest of the course, and the kind of task you took this course in order to be able to attempt at all, are made of several functions that fit together, and the difficulty is no longer in any one piece but in the fitting together. This week is about how you get an assistant to help you build something of that size without losing control of it, and the whole answer is contained in the title: you plan before you prompt.
Consider first what happens if you do not. The tempting way to use an assistant on a real task is to describe the whole thing in one prompt and ask for the complete program. You will get one. It will be a single block of code, often quite long, that appears to do what you asked. The trouble begins the moment you try to trust it. You cannot read all of it with the care you gave a four line function last week, so you skim, and skimming is how the plausible wrong code you studied slips past you. You cannot test it piece by piece, because it is not in pieces; it is one lump, and your only test is to run the whole thing and see whether the final answer looks right, which tells you nothing about the parts. And when the final answer is wrong, as it usually will be at first, you have no way to find out which part is at fault, because you never separated the parts. You are left staring at a wall of code that a machine wrote and that you do not understand, with a bug somewhere inside it and no way in. What has actually gone wrong here is subtle: by asking for everything at once, you did not merely delegate the typing to the assistant, you delegated the thinking, and the thinking is the part you cannot afford to give away.
The alternative rests on a division of labor that you must keep clear in your head. You drive; the assistant types. The thinking that matters in a program of any size is the decision about what the pieces are, what each piece is responsible for, and how they connect to each other. That thinking is yours and stays yours. What the assistant is good for is filling in the implementation of a piece once you have decided what that piece is and what it must do. It is an extremely fast, extremely fluent, and extremely unreliable typist for parts that you have specified. It is not a designer, and the surest way to get into trouble is to let it act like one.
The thinking you keep for yourself is called decomposition, and it is the same skill you learned when you first met functions, now used at a larger scale. To decompose a task is to break it into functions, each of which does one thing, has a name that says what that thing is, takes some inputs, and returns a result. A good decomposition is not measured by cleverness; it is measured by whether each piece is small enough that you can do three things with it: read it, test it, and understand it entirely on its own without holding the rest of the program in your head. If a piece is too big to test in isolation, or too tangled to understand without knowing what four other pieces are doing, the decomposition is not yet good enough, and no amount of help from the assistant will rescue a bad decomposition, because the assistant will simply fill your unclear pieces with unclear code.
The plan is where this thinking is written down, and it is written before you prompt for anything. A plan is the list of functions the task will need, and for each function, its name, what goes into it, what comes out of it, and one concrete example of an input and its correct output. You do not need a special format for this, because Python already gives you a perfect one. A plan is most naturally written as a set of empty functions with docstrings and no bodies, which is to say, exactly the kind of stub file the projects have been handing you all along. Suppose the task is to take a DNA strand and report its length, its GC content, and whether it counts as GC rich. A plan for it might look like this, written before a single line of working code exists:
def gc_content(dna):
    "Fraction of bases that are G or C. Example: gc_content('GGAT') == 0.5"
    ...

def is_gc_rich(dna):
    "True if more than half the bases are G or C, using gc_content. is_gc_rich('GGGA') == True"
    ...

def describe(dna):
    "A sentence reporting the strand's length, its GC content, and whether it is GC rich."
    ...
Look at what you have before you have asked the assistant for anything. You have decided that the task divides into three pieces and not some other number. You have named each piece and stated what goes in and what comes out. You have committed to one example per piece that you can check by hand, which means you have started deciding the awkward cases as well, because to write the example for is_gc_rich you had to decide what happens at exactly one half. You have even recorded a dependency, that is_gc_rich uses gc_content and describe uses both, so you know the order in which the pieces must be built. All of that is design, all of it is yours, and none of it required the assistant. This is what it means to plan before you prompt.
Writing the plan first, rather than after, matters for the same reason writing the tests first mattered last week. If you prompt for the code first and plan afterward, the assistant’s code becomes the thing you react to. Its choice of how to break up the problem, which may be sensible or may be strange, becomes your starting point, and you find yourself adjusting your understanding to fit its structure instead of making it fit yours. Plan first and the order of authority is correct: you decide the shape of the solution, and the assistant is asked only to fill shapes you have already drawn.
With the plan in hand, you build one piece at a time, and you verify each piece before you build the next one on top of it. You prompt the assistant for gc_content alone, you read what it gives you against the questions from last week, you run the tests you seeded from your example, and only when that piece is proven do you move on to is_gc_rich, which you can now build trusting that the gc_content underneath it is sound. Then describe, last, on top of two pieces you have already checked. The reason this is so much safer than the single lump is that it localizes everything. When something is wrong, it is wrong in the piece you are currently working on, because everything beneath it has already passed its tests, so you always know where to look. Integration, the fitting together that was the whole difficulty, becomes the almost boring act of assembling parts you have each already proven, rather than the terrifying act of debugging a whole you never understood.
Notice that the plan and the contract from last week are the same object seen at two scales. Each function’s example in the plan is the seed of that function’s test, so to plan a program is already to begin specifying it. Planning tells you what the pieces are; the tests tell you what each piece must satisfy; and building piece by piece with the tests as you go is simply the two ideas used together. When you give the assistant its instructions, you give it the context it needs and no license to wander: the plan, the signature of the one function you want now, and the example or test that function must satisfy. You ask for that one function, you verify it, and you move on. You do not let the assistant race ahead and write three functions you have not planned, because a function you did not plan is a function you did not decide you needed, and it will cost you more to understand and check than it would have cost you to write yourself.
This is exactly the method by which you will build the finale, which is deliberately larger than anything you could write unaided. That is not a threat; it is the point. The plan is what makes a task that is too big to hold in your head at once into a task you can actually do, because with a plan you never face the whole thing. You face one small, named, testable piece at a time, on top of pieces you have already proven, and the assistant does the fast typing for each piece while you do the deciding and the checking. A problem you could not have written alone becomes a sequence of problems each of which you can.

Exercise 51-1
AI: Collaborator
Do the wrong thing once, deliberately, so that you know what it feels like. Take a task made of three or four pieces, such as reading a file of DNA sequences and reporting which one has the highest GC content, and ask the assistant for the whole thing in a single prompt. Do not plan it, do not break it up. Read what comes back and then attempt exactly one thing: test one piece of it in isolation, without running the rest. Write down what stopped you. Nine times out of ten what stopped you is that there was no piece to test, because the assistant returned one lump that only produces an answer at the very end. Keep this code. You will want to compare it with what you build over the next few exercises.


Exercise 51-2
SOLO
Now practise the deciding, with no assistant and no working code at all. Take the same task and write only the plan for it, as a set of empty functions with docstrings and no bodies. The whole exercise is the decomposition: deciding what the pieces are, naming them, and stating what goes in and out of each. When you think you are done, check your plan against the standard from earlier: is each piece small enough to read, to test, and to understand on its own?


Exercise 51-3
SOLO
Strengthen the plan you just wrote by adding to each function one concrete example of an input and its correct output, worked out by hand. As you do this you will find that some functions are harder to give an example for than others, and that difficulty is information: a function you cannot easily give an example for is usually a function that is doing too much, or that you have not thought through, and it should be split or reconsidered before any code is written for it.


Exercise 51-4
AI: Collaborator
Only now let the assistant near the design, and note carefully what the badge does and does not license. Show it your stubs and your examples and ask it one narrow question: is there a case my examples do not cover, or a piece I have not named? You are not asking it to redesign anything, and you are not obliged to take anything it says. Go through its suggestions one at a time and, for each, write accept or reject and one line of reason. Rejecting a suggestion you understand is a better outcome than accepting one you do not, and the point of the exercise is to feel the difference between a collaborator, whose opinions you weigh, and a designer, whose decisions you inherit.


Exercise 51-5
AI: Collaborator
Take the discipline all the way through on a single piece. From your plan, choose one function, and only when its plan and its example are written do you allow yourself to prompt the assistant for that one function. Verify the result against your example, using the check widget or your own asserts. The rule to feel here is the one in the title of the week: the plan comes first, the prompt comes second, and the verification comes before you are allowed to believe any of it. When it passes, put it beside the single lump from the first exercise and say which of the two you would be willing to defend.
For your logbook this week, include the plan you wrote as stubs for one task, and note which function in it was hardest to write an example for and what that difficulty told you about your decomposition. If you built one of the pieces with the assistant, record whether having planned it first changed how you judged the code it gave you.

title: 52  AI: Training
text:
Learning from examples
In the last two chapters you set every weight and threshold yourself. You moved a slider, watched what happened, and moved it again until the network did what you wanted. That works for a network with ten parameters. It does not work for one with a million, and the language models behind AI assistants have hundreds of billions. Nobody sets those by hand. Nobody even knows what most of them should be. Instead, the network finds its own weights from examples, in a process called training. This chapter explains how. It turns out to be the same thing you did with the sliders, made systematic: change a weight a little, see whether the answer got better, and keep going in the direction that helps.
A neural network is trained using training data: a large number of inputs, each paired with the output you want for it. For a network that recognizes splice sites, each input is a short DNA sequence and each desired output is 1 if the sequence contains a splice site and 0 if it does not. For a network that predicts how strongly a gene is expressed from its promoter sequence, the desired output is the measured expression level. The desired output is often called the target, or the label.
At the start the weights are set to small random numbers, so the network’s outputs are nonsense. Training then repeats three things many times. It runs the network on some examples and compares its outputs with the targets. It works out, for every weight, whether making that weight a little bigger or a little smaller would bring the outputs closer to the targets. And it changes every weight a little in the helpful direction. After enough rounds, the weights settle on values that make the network do the job.

title: 52  AI: Training
text:
Measuring how wrong: the loss
To change weights in a direction that makes the network predictions less wrong, we need a way to measure how wrong the network is. For a single example, the error is the difference between the network’s output \(y\) and the target \(t\). Training uses the square of that difference, \((y - t)^2\). Squaring makes every error positive, so an output that is too high and one that is too low both count as wrong, and it makes large errors count much more than small ones: an error of 2 counts 4, an error of 10 counts 100. Averaged over all the examples, this number is called the loss. A loss of 0 means the network gets every example exactly right. The bigger the loss, the worse it does. Other kinds of loss are used for other kinds of output, but they all work the same way: one number that gets smaller as the network gets better.
For demonstration, lets try this with a “network” that is just a single neuron with one input \(x\) and one weight \(w\). To keep it simple we assume the threshold is so small that we can ignore both that and the activation function (Figure 52.1). In this simplest possible case, the output is just \(y = wx\). To make it even simpler, our training data is just a single example: input \(x = 2\), target \(t = 6\). You can see at once that the right weight is \(w = 3\), because \(3 \times 2 = 6\). The training algorithm cannot see that. All it can do is try a weight and compute the loss:
\[
L(w) = (y - t)^2 = (2w - 6)^2
\tag{52.1}\]




  
    
    
  
  
    
    
  
  
    
    
    
  
  
    x
    y
    L
  
  
    w
    t = 6
    x = 2
    y = w × 2 = 2w
    (2w − 6)²
  



Figure 52.1: The one-neuron network. The input \(x = 2\) is multiplied by the weight \(w\) to give the output \(y = 2w\), and the loss \(L\) compares \(y\) with the target \(t = 6\).



With \(w = 1\) the output is 2 and the loss is \((2 - 6)^2 = 16\). With \(w = 2\) the output is 4 and the loss is 4. With \(w = 3\) the loss is 0. Computed for every \(w\), the loss traces out the curve in Figure 52.2 and goal is to find the \(w\) that puts the loss at the bottom of that curve.








Figure 52.2: The loss \((2w - 6)^2\) of the one-neuron network for different values of its weight \(w\). The dots are the first steps of gradient descent from \(w = 1\) with a learning rate of 0.05. Each step goes downhill, and the steps get shorter as the curve flattens out near the bottom at \(w = 3\).

title: 52  AI: Training
text:
Walking downhill: gradient descent
With one weight you could simply try a lot of different values of \(w\) and pick the best. With a million weights that is of cause hopeless: trying just ten values for each would mean more combinations than there are atoms in the universe. The gradient descent training algorithm does not know what the curve looks like. All it cares about is which direction is downhill from where it is now. The steeper the downhill slope (gradient) the better. The slope of the loss curve at a given \(w\) says how much the loss changes when \(w\) is nudged a little. At \(w = 1\) the loss is \(16\). At \(w = 1.01\) the output is \(2.02\) so the loss is \((2.02 - 6)^2 = 15.8404\). So from \(w = 1\) to \(w = 1.01\), the loss went down by \(0.1596\), so the slope is \(-0.1596 / 0.01 = 15.96\).
Differentiating our simple loss function in Equation 52.1, gives the slope as a function of \(w\): \(8w - 24\). At \(w = 1\) that gives \(-16\) agreeing with the \(15.96\) computed above. Knowing the slope, the step downhill is
\[
w_{\text{new}} = w - \eta \times \text{slope}
\]
where \(\eta\) (the Greek letter eta) is the learning rate, a small number that sets how big each step is. The minus sign is what makes the step go downhill: a negative slope makes \(w\) bigger, a positive slope makes it smaller. And because the step is proportional to the slope, the steps automatically get shorter as the ground flattens out near the bottom.
With \(\eta = 0.05\) and a start at \(w = 1\), the first step gives \(w = 1 - 0.05 \times (-16) = 1.8\). At \(w = 1.8\) the slope is \(8 \times 1.8 - 24 = -9.6\), and the next step gives \(w = 1.8 + 0.48 = 2.28\). You can see the steps as dots in Figure 52.2. Here is the same thing as a small Python program. Before you run it, predict roughly where \(w\) ends up after ten steps.

x = 2               # the input of our single training example
target = 6          # the output we want for it
w = 1               # a starting guess for the weight
learning_rate = 0.05

print("{:<6}{:<10}{:<10}".format('Step', 'Weight', 'Loss'))
for step in range(15):
    y = w * x                         # run the network
    loss = (y - target) ** 2          # how wrong is it?
    slope = 2 * (y - target) * x      # which way is downhill? (this is 8w - 24)

    print("{:<6}{:<10f}{:<20f}".format(step, w, loss))

    w = w - learning_rate * slope     # take a step downhill

Step  Weight    Loss      
0     1.000000  16.000000           
1     1.800000  5.760000            
2     2.280000  2.073600            
3     2.568000  0.746496            
4     2.740800  0.268739            
5     2.844480  0.096746            
6     2.906688  0.034829            
7     2.944013  0.012538            
8     2.966408  0.004514            
9     2.979845  0.001625            
10    2.987907  0.000585            
11    2.992744  0.000211            
12    2.995646  0.000076            
13    2.997388  0.000027            
14    2.998433  0.000010            


The learning rate matters. If it is too small, training takes too long. If it is too large, and each step overshoots and lands on the other side of the valley, possibly even higher up than where it started.
In a real network the loss depends on all the weights, but the slope is still measured separately for each one. I.e., how does the loss change when one weight is nudged and all others remain the same. The list of all these slopes is the gradient. Each step of gradient descent moves every weight a little, each in its own downhill direction. Even in a landscape of million directions, this approach would still move the loss downhill. However, for a network with a billion weights, changing each weight separately would require a billion nudges just to take a single step, and since training requires millions of steps - well you can do the math. Training large networks became possible only because (Rumelhart et al., 1986) came up with a much faster way to get all the slopes at once. The algorithm is called backpropagation

title: 52  AI: Training
text:
Backpropagation
Backpropagation finds every slope in a single backward pass through the network, which costs about as much as running the network once. Take a network with two neurons in a chain, as in Figure 52.3. To keep the arithmetic simple we again assume thresholds are so small that we do not have to take them or the activation function into account. The input \(x\) goes to a hidden neuron that computes \(h = w_1 x\). \(h\) then goes to an output neuron that computes \(y = w_2 h\).
The “forward pass” is just running the network like you have done many times already. If \(x = 1\), \(w_1 = 2\), \(w_2 = 1\) and the target is \(t = 4\), then \(h = 2 \times 1 = 2\), which in turn makes \(y = 1 \times 2 = 2\), producing a loss of \((2 - 4)^2 = 4\).




  
    
    
    
  
  
    
    
    
  
  
    
    
    
    
  
  
    x
    h
    y
    L
  
  
    w₁ = 2
    w₂ = 1
    t = 4
    x = 1
    h = 2 × 1 = 2
    y = 1 × 2 = 2
    (2 − 4)² = 4
  



Figure 52.3: The forward pass through the two-neuron chain. Each value is computed from the one before it, from left to right, and the loss \(L\) compares the output \(y\) with the target \(t = 4\).



The “backward pass” starts from the end and works its way backwards, one neuron at a time. At every node, it evaluates how much the loss would change if that neuron’s value was nudged. The idea is to “propagate” the slope from the loss “backwards” across the hidden neurons, in proportion to the weight that connects them. Since the loss is \((y - t)^2\), the slope with respect to \(y\) is \(2(y - t) = 2 \times (2 - 4) = -4\). This means that if \(y\) went up by a little, the loss would go down by four times as much. That makes sense since the output \(y\) is lower than the target \(t\). Working backwards, we get to the \(w_2\) weight. Since \(y = w_2 h\), nudging \(w_2\) changes \(y\) by \(h\) times as much, so the slope for \(w_2\) is the slope for \(y\) times \(h\): \(-4 \times 2 = -8\). Nudging \(h\) changes \(y\) by \(w_2\) times as much, so the slope for \(h\) is \(-4 \times w_2 = -4 \times 1 = -4\). Finally, the weight \(w_1\). Since \(h = w_1 x\), nudging \(w_1\) changes \(h\) by \(x\) times as much, so the slope for \(w_1\) is \(-4 \times x = -4 \times 1 = -4\). Figure 52.4 collects the whole backward pass.

Figure 52.4: The backward pass. The blue arrows pass the slope back from the loss, one neuron at a time. The slope for each weight is the slope of the neuron the weight leads into, times the value that travels along the weight.



The slopes for both \(w_1\) and \(w_2\) are negative, which means gradient descent will make both weights larger. \(w_2\), has the steeper slope and will grow fastest. In a network with many layers, the slopes flow backward layer by layer, each layer doing a little local multiplication, until every weight has its slope. In mathematics this way of combining slopes along a chain is called the chain rule.
With activation functions, the slope of the activation function enters as an additional factor at every neuron. That is why a step function discussed in ?sec-nn-activation does not work well in training. Its slope is 0 everywhere (except for the jump), and multiplying by 0 stops the chain propagating slope backwards. If the slope is 0, nudging the parameters in the remaining part of the network will not affect the loss. Without this connection between loss and parameter values, we cannot train the network.
The sigmoid activation function has non-zero slope, but across many multiplications across a large network, the tiny slopes far from 0 make the numbers become near-zero anyway. ReLU works best in training because its slope is 1 wherever the neuron is active, so the slope propagates undiminished. Its slope is 0 where it is silent, so even with ReLU, a node will stop learning if it is silent for every example in the training set.

title: 52  AI: Training
text:
Backpropagation in the tiny network
The two-neuron chain left out the thresholds and the activation function to keep the arithmetic simple. Now we put them back and do a forward and a backward pass through the tiny network from ?sec-nn-tiny, set to two hidden neurons. It has one input \(x\), two hidden neurons and one output neuron. Each hidden neuron computes its net input \(z_i = w_i x - \theta_i\) and puts it through the ReLU activation function, so \(h_i = f(z_i)\), where \(f(z) = \max(0, z)\). The output neuron has no activation function, as in the widget with “Apply \(f\) at output” unticked, so it computes \(y = v_1 h_1 + v_2 h_2 - \theta\). Training must find a slope for all seven parameters: the weights \(w_1\) and \(w_2\) into the hidden layer, the hidden thresholds \(\theta_1\) and \(\theta_2\), the weights \(v_1\) and \(v_2\) into the output, and the output threshold \(\theta\).
Let us start the network from the weights \(w_1 = 1\) and \(w_2 = -1\), give both hidden neurons the threshold 1, and set \(v_1 = 2\), \(v_2 = 3\) and \(\theta = 1\). The training example is the input \(x = 2\) with the target \(t = 3\).
The forward pass works through the network from left to right. The net inputs of the hidden neurons are \(z_1 = 1 \times 2 - 1 = 1\) and \(z_2 = -1 \times 2 - 1 = -3\). ReLU lets the positive value through and turns the negative one into 0, so \(h_1 = 1\) and \(h_2 = 0\). The second hidden neuron is silent. The output is \(y = 2 \times 1 + 3 \times 0 - 1 = 1\), and the loss is \((1 - 3)^2 = 4\). Figure 52.5 shows these values in gray.

Figure 52.5: The forward and backward pass through the tiny network. The gray numbers are the values from the forward pass, and the blue numbers are the slopes from the backward pass. Next to each weight and each threshold is the slope for that parameter. Under each hidden neuron, the first blue line is the slope for its output \(h_i\), and the second is that slope passed back through ReLU, which gives the slope for its net input \(z_i\). Under the output neuron is the slope for \(y\), where the backward pass begins.



Most of the backward pass works exactly as in the two-neuron chain. The slope for \(y\) is \(2(y - t) = -4\), and the slope for each weight is the slope of whatever the weight leads into, times the value that travels along the weight. Figure 52.5 shows all of these products. Four things are new, and they are what this example is for.
The first is that the output neuron receives two inputs. The backward pass sends the slope for \(y\) back along both incoming edges, and each branch gets the slope for \(y\) times its own weight: \(-4 \times v_1 = -8\) for \(h_1\) and \(-4 \times v_2 = -12\) for \(h_2\). The two branches do not affect each other. Each is computed as if the other were not there, and from here on the backward pass simply follows each branch on its own. An output neuron with a hundred inputs would send the same slope back along a hundred edges in the same way.
The second is the thresholds. A threshold is subtracted from the net input, so nudging it up by a little moves the net input down by the same amount. That is a factor of \(-1\), and the slope for a threshold is minus the slope of the net input it belongs to. For the output threshold that gives \(-4 \times (-1) = 4\), and for \(\theta_1\) it gives \(-8 \times (-1) = 8\). Both are positive, so gradient descent will make both thresholds smaller, which makes the neurons fire more easily and raises the output, as it should since the output is too low. In this way a threshold behaves just like a weight on an input that is always \(-1\), and training treats it as one.
The third is the activation function. To get from \(h_i\) back to the net input \(z_i\), the slope has to pass through ReLU, and nudging \(z_i\) changes \(h_i\) by the slope of ReLU at \(z_i\). Where \(z\) is positive, ReLU passes its input straight through, so its slope is 1. Where \(z\) is negative, the output stays at 0 however \(z\) is nudged, so its slope is 0. The first hidden neuron is active, and its slope passes through unchanged: \(-8 \times 1 = -8\). The second is silent, and its slope is stopped: \(-12 \times 0 = 0\). Everything behind it, \(w_2\) and \(\theta_2\), gets a slope of 0 too, and so does \(v_2\), because the value traveling along it is \(h_2 = 0\). This is a pity, because \(h_2\) had the steepest slope of all, so if the second neuron fired it could do the most to raise \(y\). For this one example that does no harm, but a neuron that is silent for every example in the training data never gets a slope and never learns. This is the dead neuron from ?sec-nn-relu. With the sigmoid instead of ReLU, the factor would be the slope of the sigmoid at \(z\), which is never more than \(0.25\), so the slope would shrink a little at every neuron it passes.
The fourth is that \(x\) feeds both hidden neurons. Nudging \(x\) would change \(z_1\) and \(z_2\) at the same time, so the slope for \(x\) is the sum of the slopes coming back along the two edges: \(-8 \times w_1 + 0 \times w_2 = -8\). Training never needs this slope, because \(x\) is the input and not a parameter. In a network with more than one hidden layer, though, every hidden neuron feeds every neuron in the next layer, just as \(x\) does here, and its slope is the sum of the slopes coming back along all its outgoing edges. Multiplying along each edge and adding where edges meet is all backpropagation ever does, however large the network.
The slopes that are not 0 all ask for a higher output: \(w_1\) and \(v_1\) will get larger, and \(\theta_1\) and \(\theta\) smaller. Training a real network is this, repeated. The forward pass computes every value, the backward pass computes every slope, and every parameter takes a small step downhill. The networks behind AI assistants have many more layers and billions of parameters, but every neuron in them does the same small local multiplications.

title: 52  AI: Training
text:
Training in practice
The network usually doesn’t run on all the training data at every step. Instead, it computes the loss and the slopes from just a random uses a small random handful of examples, called a batch, and. The step is a little less accurate, but there are far more of them for the same amount of computing, and the noise from the random batches even helps the network avoid getting stuck. One pass through all the training data is called an epoch, and training usually runs for many epochs.
The loss function of a real network isn’t a neat bowl like the one in Figure 52.2, but a landscape with countless hills, ridges, and valleys. Gradient descent finds only the bottom of the valley it happens to walk into, which may not be the deepest. For large networks, this matters less than you might fear: there are so many directions to move that a true dead end is rare, and many different sets of weights work about equally well.
The most important practical point is how to tell whether training worked. A network with enough parameters can drive its training-data loss almost to zero by memorizing it, like a student memorizing the answers to last year’s exam without understanding the subject. This is called overfitting, and a network that has overfitted does well on its training examples and badly on everything else. The only way to find out is to test the network on examples it has never seen. Before training starts, part of the data is therefore set aside as a test set, and the network is judged on that alone. It is the same principle you have used with code all term: the program is not right because it looks right, or because it works on the example you wrote it for. It is right when it passes tests it was not built to pass.
Even a network that does well on a test set has only learned what was in the data, and it learns whatever reduces the loss, including shortcuts nobody intended. A network trained to detect pneumonia in chest X-rays from several hospitals turned out to rely partly on features that identified which hospital an image came from, since the hospitals differed in how common pneumonia was among their patients. It generally did worse on X-rays from hospitals it had not been trained on (Zech et al., 2018). The loss rewards getting the training answers right, not getting them right for the right reasons.

Exercise 52-1
SOLO
Continue gradient descent for the one-neuron network by hand, with \(x = 2\), \(t = 6\) and \(\eta = 0.05\). You have reached \(w = 2.28\). Work out each answer on paper before you open it.






TipWhat is the slope at \(w = 2.28\)?





\(8 \times 2.28 - 24 = -5.76\). It is still negative, so the next step increases \(w\), but it is less steep than before because you are closer to the bottom.









TipWhat is the next value of \(w\)?





\(2.28 - 0.05 \times (-5.76) = 2.28 + 0.288 = 2.568\). This should match step 3 in the output of the program above.









TipHow far is \(w\) from 3 now, compared with one step ago?





It was \(3 - 2.28 = 0.72\) and is now \(3 - 2.568 = 0.432\), which is \(0.6\) times as far. Every step with this learning rate leaves \(0.6\) of the remaining distance.






Exercise 52-2
SOLO
Type the training program from ?sec-train-descent into a file or a notebook cell (do not copy and paste it) and run it to check that you get the same output. Then change the learning rate. For each change, predict what will happen to \(w\) before you run the program.






TipSet the learning rate to \(0.01\). What happens?





The weight still moves toward 3, but much more slowly: each step leaves \(0.92\) of the remaining distance, so after ten steps \(w\) has only reached about \(2.13\). A small learning rate is safe but slow.









TipSet the learning rate to \(0.25\). What happens?





The weight jumps from 1 to 5, then back to 1, then to 5 again, forever, and the loss stays at 16. Each step goes exactly as far past the bottom as it started before it. The step is so long that it jumps across the valley to the same height on the other side.









TipSet the learning rate to \(0.3\). What happens?





It gets worse with every step. The weight goes from 1 to 5.8, then to \(-0.92\), and on to ever larger values on alternate sides of 3, and the loss grows quickly instead of shrinking. Each step overshoots so far that it lands higher up the other side of the valley. When the loss of a real network suddenly grows during training, a learning rate that is too large is the first thing to suspect.






Exercise 52-3
SOLO
Do the forward and backward pass for the two-neuron chain from ?sec-train-backprop by hand, but now with \(x = 2\), \(w_1 = 1\), \(w_2 = 3\) and target \(t = 5\).






TipWhat are \(h\), \(y\) and the loss?





\(h = 1 \times 2 = 2\), \(y = 3 \times 2 = 6\), and the loss is \((6 - 5)^2 = 1\).









TipWhat are the slopes for \(y\), \(w_2\), \(h\) and \(w_1\)?





For \(y\): \(2 \times (6 - 5) = 2\). For \(w_2\): \(2 \times h = 2 \times 2 = 4\). For \(h\): \(2 \times w_2 = 2 \times 3 = 6\). For \(w_1\): \(6 \times x = 6 \times 2 = 12\).









TipWhich way will gradient descent move each weight, and which will move most?





Both slopes are positive, so both weights will be made smaller, which makes sense because the output is too high. The slope for \(w_1\) is three times steeper than the slope for \(w_2\), so \(w_1\) will change most.

Compute the loss with \(w_1 = 1\) and with \(w_1 = 1.01\), keeping everything else the same, and divide the difference by \(0.01\):

loss_after = (w2 * (1.01 * x) - t) ** 2
print((loss_after - loss_before) / 0.01)
This prints a number close to 12 (about 12.36; the nudge is small but not infinitely small, so the result is not exact).

Filling in the dynamic programming matrix
This chapter is about global pairwise alignment, and you will implement your own Needleman-Wunch algorithm.
Your task is to find an optimal alignment of two sequences. If two such sequences are roughly 140 bases long, there are as many different ways to align them as there are atoms in the visible universe. Finding an optimal alignment among those \(10^{80}\) possibilities is a hard problem, but implementing the Needleman-Wunch algorithm will let you do it.
